x-m-h2-01.title: Find the line where the logarithmic equation solution has a problem
x-m-h2-01.goal: Find and fix the problem caused by not checking the argument condition in a solution to a logarithmic equation.
x-m-h2-01.material: Minho solved the equation log₂(x−1) + log₂(x−3) = 3 and answered, ‘The solutions are x=5 and x=−1, two of them.’ Read aloud, it is ‘log base 2 of (x minus 1) plus log base 2 of (x minus 3) equals 3’.
x-m-h2-01.thinking.0: Check each line of the solution
x-m-h2-01.thinking.1: Find the condition that was missing from the solution
x-m-h2-01.thinking.2: Fix the answer and explain why
x-m-h2-01.prereq.0: The meaning and basic properties of logarithms
x-m-h2-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Minho's solution that has a problem. (If several lines in a row are a problem, you may choose just one of them.)
x-m-h2-01.s.s1.hint.0: Each time the expression changes, read while checking that it means the same as the previous line.
x-m-h2-01.s.s1.line.5: So the solutions are x = 5 and x = −1, two of them.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.prompt: Tell Minho the correct solution and the reason. Include what problem happens when you put x=−1 into the original equation.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.hint.0: Read while checking the reason the expression was changed in each line.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put x=−1 and x=5 each into the arguments of the logarithms in the original equation and check what the values become.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain why x=−1 cannot be a solution using the value of the argument?
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say what condition was needed before the expression was changed?
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you put x=5 into the original equation to check that it satisfies it?
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.model.0: The only solution is x=5. If I put in x=−1, the argument is negative like log₂(−2), so it is not defined. So only 5, which satisfies the argument condition x>3, is a solution.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.model.1: When solving the equation, the arguments must always be positive. x−1>0 and x−3>0, so x>3 is needed, and x=−1 is not in this range, so it must be thrown out. So the answer is x=5.
x-m-h2-01.s.s1.hint.1: Put the values at the end of the solution directly into the equation in the first line. What happens to the value inside the logarithm?
x-m-h2-01.s.s1.explain: The first place where it goes off is line 2. When the sum of the two logarithms is combined into one logarithm, the argument conditions x−1>0 and x−3>0 disappear from the expression, and those conditions were not written down separately. So in line 5 both roots were accepted, and line 6 is that conclusion. The argument must be positive, so x>3 is required. If x=−1, then x−1=−2 and x−3=−4, the arguments are negative, so the equation is not defined. If x=5, log₂4 + log₂2 = 2+1 = 3, so it holds. So the solution is the single value x=5.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.model.2: From the argument conditions x−1>0 and x−3>0, x>3. x=−1 is out of range, so discard it, and the answer is 5.
x-m-h2-01.s.s2.model.3: The answer is 5. Putting in x=−1 gives log₂(−2), which is not defined, so it is not a solution.

x-m-h2-02.title: Is a power of 2 always greater than the square of x?
x-m-h2-02.goal: Find a counterexample to the claim that 2ˣ>x² always holds, and judge why you can say from which value it holds.
x-m-h2-02.material: Seojin saw that when x=1, 2¹=2>1², and when x=5, 2⁵=32>5²=25, and said, ‘For a positive integer x, 2ˣ is always greater than x².’ (2ˣ is the number you get by multiplying 2 by itself x times, and x² is the number you get by multiplying x twice.)
x-m-h2-02.thinking.1: Tell apart checking some cases from explaining why
x-m-h2-02.prereq.0: The meaning of exponents and calculating powers
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.prompt: Find two different positive integers x that show Seojin's statement is wrong. (That is, x for which 2ˣ is not greater than x², that is, 2ˣ ≤ x².)
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.hint.0: Put in x=1, 2, 3, ... in order and write the values of 2ˣ and x² side by side.
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Look at the values between x=1 and x=5 that Seojin checked.
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.fail.c1: x must be an integer that is at least 1.
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.fail.c2: For this x, 2ˣ is greater than x². It is not a value that breaks Seojin's statement.
x-m-h2-02.s.s1.explain: If x=2, then 2²=4=2²; if x=3, then 2³=8<9=3²; if x=4, then 2⁴=16=4². These three are counterexamples. At x=1 or x=5, 2ˣ is greater.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.prompt: Now you want to say, ‘For every integer x that is at least 5, 2ˣ>x².’ Which is the most valid reason that this always holds?
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Tell apart whether each choice says ‘why it is so for every x’ or only says ‘how many cases were checked’.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write in a table how many times larger each of the two values becomes when going from x=5 to 6 and 7.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.o.a: I calculated one by one from x=5 to x=20 and found 2ˣ>x² every time with no exceptions
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.r.a: Even if you check 20 cases, you cannot know whether the next value holds. Checking some cases is evidence, not a reason.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.o.b: When x increases by 1, 2ˣ doubles, and x² grows by less than double (for x≥3)
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.r.b: This compares how much each of the two values grows at each step and finds why the gap keeps widening.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.o.c: 2ˣ is an exponential function and x² is a polynomial function, so 2ˣ is greater from 5 on
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.r.c: It is true that an exponential function eventually becomes larger, but it was not so from the start, as at x=3. This does not explain from where.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.o.d: If you draw the graphs, the graph of 2ˣ is above the graph of x²
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.r.d: A graph helps with guessing, but where the two graphs are very close it is hard to tell by eye, and it does not explain the reason.
x-m-h2-02.s.s2.explain: At x=5, 2⁵=32>25, and when x increases by 1, 2ˣ doubles while x² becomes (x+1)²/x² times, which is less than 2 when x≥3. So once it gets ahead, the gap keeps widening. Checking some values, the kind of function, or the shape of a graph alone does not explain ‘every x’.

x-m-h2-03.title: Can sinθ=3/5 alone tell us tanθ?
x-m-h2-03.goal: Find for yourself a case where the given information does not fix a single value, and pick out the information needed to fix the value.
x-m-h2-03.material: Jihu said only that ‘sinθ=3/5 for an angle θ’ and asked for the value of tanθ. Daeun said, ‘There is not enough information,’ and Hyunwoo said, ‘It is enough.’ How to read: sinθ is sine theta, cosθ is cosine theta, tanθ is tangent theta, and 3/5 is three fifths.
x-m-h2-03.thinking.1: Decide whether the information is enough
x-m-h2-03.prereq.0: The definitions of trigonometric functions and basic relations
x-m-h2-03.prereq.1: Where an angle lies by quadrant
x-m-h2-03.s.s1.prompt: When there is an angle θ with sinθ=3/5, find two different possible pairs of values (cosθ, tanθ). (Enter cosθ=c and tanθ=t; you may write decimals. e.g. 3/5=0.6)
x-m-h2-03.s.s1.hint.0: Put sinθ=0.6 into sin²θ+cos²θ=1 and write what the equation for cosθ becomes.
x-m-h2-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many values of cosθ satisfy that equation, and calculate tanθ=sinθ÷cosθ for each.
x-m-h2-03.s.s1.fail.c1: It does not make sin²θ+cos²θ=1. Check what the square of cosθ must be when sinθ=0.6.
x-m-h2-03.s.s1.explain: If sinθ=3/5, then cos²θ=16/25, so cosθ=4/5 or −4/5. If cosθ=0.8, tanθ=0.75, and if cosθ=−0.8, tanθ=−0.75, so two cases are possible.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.prompt: If you are also told one of the following in addition to sinθ=3/5, the value of tanθ is fixed to one. Choose all such pieces of information.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether each of the two cases you found in the previous step satisfies the condition in each choice.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.hint.1: Separate the choices where both cases satisfy the condition from the choices where only one case remains.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.a: A positive angle can be in any quadrant. Check whether both of the cases you made earlier remain.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.o.b: θ is an angle in the second quadrant
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.b: This condition leaves only one of the two cases. Look at the sign of cosθ in the second quadrant.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.o.c: θ is an angle in the first or second quadrant
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.c: If sinθ=3/5>0, you already know this, so it is not new information. Both cases remain.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.d: If sinθ>0 and tanθ<0, the sign of cosθ is fixed. Check which of the two earlier cases remains.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.e: This range includes both the first and second quadrants, so both cases remain.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.r.f: It tells you the sign of cosθ directly, so only one of the two cases remains.
x-m-h2-03.s.s2.explain: If sinθ=3/5, then cosθ=±4/5, so if you know the sign of cosθ, tanθ is fixed. Second quadrant, tanθ<0 (cosθ<0 since sinθ>0), and cosθ<0 all mean cosθ<0, so tanθ=−3/4 is fixed. For the others, the case cosθ>0 remains, so there are two values of tanθ.

x-m-h2-04.title: How many triangles can be made from two sides and one angle?
x-m-h2-04.goal: Test the generalization ‘there are always two’ with specific values and explain with reasons in which cases it does not hold.
x-m-h2-04.material: In triangle ABC, ∠A=60° and the length of side BC is a=7. When the length of side CA, b, is given, you can fix the length c of side AB and make a triangle. (a, b, c are the sides opposite ∠A, ∠B, ∠C. cos60°=1/2.) Gaeun said, ‘If b is greater than 7, two such triangles are always made.’
x-m-h2-04.thinking.0: Make cases that satisfy the conditions yourself
x-m-h2-04.thinking.1: Choose values that refute the claim
x-m-h2-04.prereq.0: Trigonometric ratios and the relationship between sides and angles in a triangle
x-m-h2-04.prereq.1: The number of roots of a quadratic equation
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.prompt: Make triangles that fit the conditions when b=8. Find two different possible lengths c of side AB.
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.hint.0: Put a=7, b=8, cos60°=1/2 into the law of cosines and write the equation for c.
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.hint.1: Choose all the solutions of that equation that can be used as a side length.
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.fail.c1: A side length must be greater than 0.
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.fail.c2: The equation you get by putting a=7, b=8 into the law of cosines a²=b²+c²−2bc·cos60° does not hold.
x-m-h2-04.s.s1.explain: From 49=64+c²−8c, c²−8c+15=0, (c−3)(c−5)=0, so c=3 or 5. Both values are positive, so two triangles can be made.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose all values of b that can be used to refute Gaeun's statement (if b is greater than 7, there are always two triangles). For each b, set up the equation for c in the same way.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.hint.0: For each b, rearrange 49=b²+c²−bc as a quadratic in c.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check with the discriminant whether the rearranged equation has real roots, and also check whether the value is within the condition b>7.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.a: It becomes c²−10c+51=0, which has no real roots. This is a case where no triangle can be made at all.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.b: b=5 is outside the condition ‘b is greater than 7’, so it does not refute Gaeun's statement.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.c: b=8 is a case where two triangles are made, so it supports Gaeun's statement.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.d: It becomes c²−12c+95=0, which has no real roots. No triangle can be made at all.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.e: b=7 is not included in the condition ‘greater than 7’. It is a case unrelated to Gaeun's statement.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.r.f: It becomes c²−9c+32=0, which has no real roots. No triangle can be made.
x-m-h2-04.s.s2.explain: By the law of cosines, 49=b²+c²−bc, that is, c²−bc+(b²−49)=0. For two different positive solutions to come out, the discriminant 196−3b² must be positive and b>7, so b must be less than about 8.08. For b=9, 10, 12 there are no real roots, so no triangle can be made at all. b=5 and 7 are outside the condition b>7.
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.prompt: Answer Gaeun in one or two sentences. Explain with examples how many triangles are made depending on the value of b.
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare the result for b=8 that you found above with the results for other values of b (for example 9, 10).
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.hint.1: Set up the equation for c in the same way and count how many suitable positive values of c there are.
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check, with the equation for c, how many triangles there are for the value of b you gave?
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you mention both the case with two triangles and the case with none?
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain, even roughly, why triangles stop being made as b gets larger?
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.model.0: Not always. If b=8, c=3 and 5, so there are two, but if b=10, the equation for c has no solution, so no triangle is made.
x-m-h2-04.s.s3.model.1: No. If b gets too large, no triangle is made. If b is 9 or 10, the quadratic equation for c has no real roots, so it does not work. There are two only when b is a little greater than 7, like b=8.

x-m-h2-05.title: 1, 2, 4, 8, … What is the next number?
x-m-h2-05.goal: See a rule guessed from the first few terms break with new data, and revise your judgment.
x-m-h2-05.material: If you mark n points on a circle and connect every two points with a line segment, the circle is divided into several regions. Mark the points so that no three line segments meet at one point. Call the number of regions aₙ. (Without a picture: with 1 point there are no segments, so there is 1 region, and with 2 points one segment divides the circle into two.)
x-m-h2-05.thinking.0: Guess a rule from some terms
x-m-h2-05.thinking.1: Revise your judgment with new data
x-m-h2-05.thinking.2: Say the difference between a guess and a proof
x-m-h2-05.prereq.0: The meaning of a sequence and its terms
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a prediction or judgment.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, separate what you can say from the data so far from what you do not know yet.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.hint.1: When new data come out, put them side by side with your first prediction and compare whether it was right.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.info: When I counted directly with 1, 2, 3, and 4 points, the numbers of regions were 1, 2, 4, 8.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you predict for the number of regions when there are 5 points?
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.after: Looking only at the first four terms, the doubling rule is the simplest guess. But you cannot be sure of a rule from a few terms.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It will be 16. It keeps doubling
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Looking only at the first four terms, the doubling rule is the simplest guess.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It will be 12. It increases by 4 each time
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.b: In 1, 2, 4, 8, the differences are 1, 2, 4, which keep growing. The rule of 4 each time does not match the data.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It seems it will be 16, but it is hard to be certain before counting directly
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You are thinking of guessing and checking as separate.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.info: I marked 5 points and counted directly, and it was 16.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.ask: What do you think when there are 6 points?
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.after: It fit up to the fifth term, so your confidence has grown, but it is still only evidence.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It is 32. It fit up to 5, so the doubling rule has been confirmed
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Fitting up to 5 makes you trust it more, but you cannot be sure from that alone.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: It is likely 32, but I will not be certain until I count the 6-point case directly
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You told apart how strong the guess is from being certain.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It could be less than 32, so I will count the 6-point case directly
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You are leaving open that the rule might break and trying to test it.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.info: When I counted the 6-point case directly, it was 31. (Note: with 7 points it is 57.)
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: What do you think about the rule ‘aₙ=2ⁿ⁻¹ (2 to the power n−1)’?
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.after: The sequence goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31, 57, so the doubling rule is not the rule of this sequence.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: At the 6th term it was 31, so this rule does not fit this sequence. Even if the first several terms are the same, it is not the same sequence
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You accepted that one counterexample breaks a rule.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Only n=6 is an exception, and the rest are 2ⁿ⁻¹
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: At n=7 it is 57, which differs from 2⁶=64, so there is more than one exception.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It fit up to 5, so the 6th one must have been counted wrong
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You do not trust the result and try to keep the rule. You can check the counting again, but 57 does not fit the rule either.
x-m-h2-05.s.s1.reflect: At first the doubling rule looked plausible, but it broke with the new data (n=6). A guess made from a few terms is only evidence until it is confirmed, and to trust a rule you need an explanation of why it holds for every n.
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.prompt: Write why you cannot fix a rule just because the first few terms are the same, and what more you need to believe the rule is right.
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.hint.0: Put the numbers of regions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 31 side by side with your first prediction.
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.hint.1: Think about how ‘having checked’ a rule differs from ‘having explained the reason’.
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you point out the specific value where the rule broke (n=6, 31)?
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you tell apart ‘checking more terms’ from ‘explaining the reason’?
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say how you revised your first prediction?
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.model.0: Even though the first five terms 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 are the same as the doubling rule, the sixth term is 31, so the rule broke. You must not fix a rule by looking at only a few terms; you need a reason (proof) why it holds for every n.
x-m-h2-05.s.s2.model.1: Checking some terms is evidence, not certainty. This sequence is 31 at n=6, so the rule of powers of 2 was wrong. To trust a rule, you have to be able to explain why it holds for all terms.

x-m-h2-06.title: Check a solution that found the general term from the sum of a sequence
x-m-h2-06.goal: Find and fix the problem in a solution that finds the general term from the sum Sₙ of a sequence, and find for yourself the condition under which it can be written as one formula.
x-m-h2-06.material: This is Seoa's solution for finding the general term when the sum Sₙ of the first n terms of a sequence {aₙ} is Sₙ = n² + 2n + 1. (Read Sₙ as ‘S sub n’, aₙ as ‘a sub n’, and Sₙ₋₁ as ‘S sub n minus 1’.)
x-m-h2-06.thinking.0: Check each line of the solution
x-m-h2-06.thinking.1: Tell apart formulas that apply in different ranges
x-m-h2-06.prereq.0: The meaning of the sum Sₙ and the general term aₙ of a sequence
x-m-h2-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in Seoa's solution that has a problem. (If several lines in a row are a problem, you may choose just one of them.)
x-m-h2-06.s.s1.hint.0: Compare whether the condition (the range of n) at the start of each line is the same as the range in the final conclusion.
x-m-h2-06.s.s1.hint.1: Find the first term a₁ directly from the definition of Sₙ, and compare it with the value in line 5.
x-m-h2-06.s.s1.line.3: So for all natural numbers n, aₙ = 2n + 1
x-m-h2-06.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the problem. Line 1 said n≥2, so aₙ=2n+1 is a formula obtained only for n≥2. The first term must be found separately: a₁=S₁=1+2+1=4, which differs from 2·1+1=3. So a₁=3 in line 5 is also wrong.
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.prompt: Write the correct general term and explain what Seoa missed.
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.hint.0: The formula for finding a₁ is defined differently from aₙ=Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁. Recall the meaning of the first term.
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the value of 2n+1 at n=1 with the value of S₁.
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you find a₁ from S₁ rather than from aₙ=Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁?
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say that you have to check whether the formula found for n≥2 also works for n=1?
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write the general term in two cases rather than as one formula?
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.model.0: a₁=S₁=4, and for n≥2, aₙ=2n+1. Seoa did not check whether the formula found for n≥2 also works for n=1. Putting in n=1 gives 3, which differs from a₁=4.
x-m-h2-06.s.s2.model.1: The general term must be written in two parts: a₁=4, and aₙ=2n+1 (n≥2). S₁=4, but putting n=1 into 2n+1 gives 3, so they are not equal. The first term has to be found separately.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.prompt: For Sₙ = p·n² + q·n + r (p, q, r are integers, p≠0), find three different (p, q, r) for which the value you get by putting n=1 into the formula found for n≥2 equals a₁, so that the general term can be written as one formula.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.hint.0: For Sₙ=pn²+qn+r, write Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁ for n≥2 in terms of p and q.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the value you get by putting n=1 into that formula with S₁=p+q+r.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.ok.c1: p is an integer that is not 0.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.fail.c1: p, q, r are integers and p must not be 0.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.ok.c2: The value of the formula found for n≥2 at n=1 is equal to a₁=S₁.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.fail.c2: The value p+q of the formula p(2n−1)+q found for n≥2 at n=1 is not equal to S₁=p+q+r.
x-m-h2-06.s.s3.explain: For n≥2, aₙ=Sₙ−Sₙ₋₁=p(2n−1)+q, so putting in n=1 gives p+q. a₁=S₁=p+q+r, so they are equal only when r=0. Sₙ=n²+2n+1 has r=1, so the first term had to be handled separately.

x-m-h2-07.title: Is ∞−∞ equal to 0? Checking two friends' claims
x-m-h2-07.goal: Test two claims with numerical calculation, explain where the intuitive reasoning went wrong, and then find the limit using algebra.
x-m-h2-07.material: Minsu said, ‘As x gets endlessly large, √(x²+x) gets close to x, so √(x²+x) − x gets close to 0.’ Seoa said, ‘It does not get close to 0, it gets close to some positive number.’ How to read: √(x²+x) is root of x squared plus x, and ‘x gets endlessly large’ is x→∞.
x-m-h2-07.thinking.0: Test the claims with numerical evidence
x-m-h2-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a limit as x gets endlessly large
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put x=100 and x=1000 into √(x²+x)−x and calculate.
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.hint.1: Make x even larger and observe which way the value moves.
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.ok.c1: x is an integer that is at least 100.
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.fail.c1: x must be an integer that is at least 100.
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.explain: For x=100 it is about 0.4988, for x=1000 about 0.49988, and for x=10000 about 0.49999. Even if you make x larger, it does not get close to 0 and stays near 0.5.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.prompt: Looking at the calculation results, which of Minsu's and Seoa's statements is better supported? Choose the most valid explanation.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.hint.0: Put the values calculated at the three values of x side by side and see how the value changes as x gets larger.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.hint.1: Tell apart whether ‘gets close’ is about a ratio or about a difference.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.o.a: Seoa's statement is supported. The difference gathers around a value that is not 0
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.r.a: Even when x was made larger, the value did not change near 0.5, so it is evidence against the claim that it is 0.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.o.b: Minsu is right. The ratio gets close to 1, so the difference gets close to 0 too
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.r.b: The ratio getting close to 1 does not mean the difference gets close to 0. For example, the ratio of x and x+0.5 gets close to 1, but the difference is always 0.5.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.r.c: When you change x and the values gather around the same value (near 0.5), it is hard to treat it as an error.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.o.d: You can't tell either way. Calculation can't tell you anything
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.r.d: Numbers do not prove the limit, but they are evidence against the claim of ‘0’.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.explain: The calculated values gather near 0.5 even as x gets larger, so Seoa's statement is supported. But numbers are only evidence, and to check exactly what the value is, you need to transform the expression.
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.prompt: Write why Minsu's reasoning ‘√(x²+x) gets close to x, so the difference is 0’ is wrong, and find the value of the limit by transforming the expression.
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write what the numerator becomes when you multiply and divide √(x²+x)−x by √(x²+x)+x.
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.hint.1: Divide the numerator and denominator by x, then see what value each part gets close to as x gets endlessly large.
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you tell apart two values getting close and the difference of two values going to 0?
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did the transformation you did turn the expression into a form where the limit can be found?
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Do the value you saw by calculation (0.4999…) and the limit you found match?
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.model.0: Getting close to x means the ratio gets close to 1, not that the difference becomes 0. Rationalizing the numerator gives x/(√(x²+x)+x)=1/(√(1+1/x)+1), and as x→∞ it is 1/2.
x-m-h2-07.s.s3.model.1: Even if √(x²+x) looks similar to x, there is still a difference between the two numbers, so I must not change it to x−x=0. Multiplying the numerator and denominator by the conjugate √(x²+x)+x gives x/(√(x²+x)+x), and the limit is 0.5 (=1/2).
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.prompt: You may use a calculator. Choose three integers x that are at least 100, calculate the value of √(x²+x) − x, round it to three decimal places, and enter it as (x, value). Entering three different x completes it. (If Minsu's claim is right, this value should get closer to 0 the larger x is.)
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.ok.c2: The value you entered matches the calculated result of √(x²+x)−x.
x-m-h2-07.s.s1.fail.c2: The value you entered is different from the calculated result. Calculate √(x²+x)−x again with a calculator and round to three decimal places.
x-m-h2-07.s.s2.o.c: Minsu is right. The value being greater than 0 is a calculator error

x-m-h2-08.title: From average speed to instantaneous speed
x-m-h2-08.goal: Shrink the interval, see what value the average speed gets close to, and organize the meaning of instantaneous speed yourself.
x-m-h2-08.material: A ball rolling down a slope moves a distance (in meters) of s(t) = t² in t seconds. You want to know the ball's speed ‘at that moment’ when t=1 second. But speed is (distance moved)÷(time taken), and at an ‘instant’ the time taken is 0, so it seems you cannot divide.
x-m-h2-08.thinking.0: Interpret the average rate of change
x-m-h2-08.thinking.2: Organize the meaning of the instantaneous rate of change
x-m-h2-08.prereq.0: The meaning of the average rate of change (average speed)
x-m-h2-08.prereq.1: The meaning of the limit of a function
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.prompt: The data are revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.hint.0: Write the length of the interval and the average speed side by side from the revealed data.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether your prediction and the new value agree, and if not, think about what you missed.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.info: The average speed over the interval [1, 3] seconds is (9−1)÷2 = 4 m/s.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you judge about the speed at the instant t=1 second?
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.after: If the interval is long, the speed changes during it, so the average speed is different from the speed at one instant. Let's shorten the interval.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It is 4 m/s. The average speed is the speed at that instant
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.r.a: If the speed changes within the interval, you cannot say the average speed equals the speed at the starting instant.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.o.b: I can't say yet. I need to find the average speed over shorter intervals starting at 1 second too
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Rather than settling one instant with a single average over a long interval, you try to check with narrower intervals.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I can't know. At an instant the time is 0, so the speed cannot be defined
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You cannot divide right away over an interval of time 0, but there is a way to approach it with short intervals.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.info: The average speed over the interval [1, 2] is 3, over [1, 1.5] it is (2.25−1)÷0.5 = 2.5, and over [1, 1.1] it is (1.21−1)÷0.1 = 2.1 m/s.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.ask: If you shrink the interval even more, like [1, 1.01], [1, 1.001], what happens to the average speed?
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.after: [1, 1.01] gives (1.0201−1)÷0.01 = 2.01, and [1, 1.001] gives 2.001. Both the numerator and the denominator get close to 0, but the ratio gathers toward 2.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.o.a: It gets close to 0. Because the length of the interval gets close to 0
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You looked only at the length of the interval. The distance moved also gets small together, so you have to look at the ratio.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.r.b: While shrinking from [1, 1.5] to [1, 1.1], it kept decreasing from 2.5 to 2.1.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You guessed the value it gathers around from the trend of the average speed decreasing: 3, 2.5, 2.1.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.info: In general, the average speed over the interval [1, 1+h] is ((1+h)²−1)÷h = 2+h (h≠0).
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.ask: When h gets endlessly close to 0 without being 0, how is it appropriate to define the instantaneous speed at t=1 second?
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.after: The instantaneous speed is the value 2 that the average speed 2+h gets close to as h→0. This value is called the derivative at t=1.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It is 2+h. It depends on h
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.r.a: h is the length of the interval, and the instantaneous speed is the one value approached as the interval shrinks.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.o.b: It can't be determined. Putting in h=0 gives 0÷0
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.r.b: The original expression ((1+h)²−1)÷h is not defined at h=0, but you can think about the value the simplified 2+h gets close to.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.o.c: It is 2. It is the value the average speed 2+h gets close to as h gets endlessly close to 0
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Instead of substituting h=0, you took as the instantaneous speed the place the value gets close to while h gets close to 0.
x-m-h2-08.s.s1.reflect: At first you thought of the average speed 4 over a long interval as the instantaneous speed, but when you saw in the data that shrinks the interval that the value gathers at 2, you revised your judgment. The instantaneous rate of change is not 0÷0, but the value that the average rate of change gets close to.
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.prompt: Write how you revised the judgment that took the average speed 4 over the interval [1, 3] as the speed at t=1 second.
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.hint.0: Write one thing that changed between your first judgment and your last judgment.
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.hint.1: Write how the length of the interval over which you calculated the average speed changed.
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write the first judgment (4) and the later judgment (2) in comparison?
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you use the average speed values (2.5, 2.1, etc.) as evidence?
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you say why a long interval makes it different from the instantaneous speed?
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.model.0: At first I took the average speed 4 over [1,3] as the speed at that instant, but when the interval is long, the speed changes in the middle, so it did not fit. When I shrank the interval to 1.5 and 1.1, the average speeds 2.5 and 2.1 got close to 2, so I revised my thinking to say the instantaneous speed is 2.
x-m-h2-08.s.s2.model.1: The shorter the interval gets, the closer the average speed gets to a single instant. 2.1, 2.01, 2.001 get endlessly close to 2, so I take the speed at t=1 to be 2. The reason I first thought it was 4 is that the interval was too long.

x-m-h2-09.title: Is a point where the derivative is 0 always an extremum?
x-m-h2-09.goal: Make a counterexample yourself to the claim ‘if the derivative is 0, there is an extremum’, and organize the conditions needed for an extremum.
x-m-h2-09.material: A student said, ‘For the cubic function f(x)=x³+ax²+bx, if there is a c with f'(c)=0, then it always has an extremum (a local maximum or local minimum) at x=c.’ (f' is the derivative of f, and f'(x)=3x²+2ax+b. An extremum is the value of the function at a point where it changes from increasing to decreasing, or from decreasing to increasing.)
x-m-h2-09.thinking.1: Judge whether the condition is sufficient
x-m-h2-09.prereq.0: The meaning of the derivative and differentiating polynomial functions
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.prompt: Find three different pairs of integers a, b for which f has a c with f'(c)=0 but no extremum (it is not decreasing on any interval), to make counterexamples.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.hint.0: Picture the graph of f'(x)=3x²+2ax+b (a parabola opening upward). For f to have an extremum, the sign of f' must change.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how this parabola must meet the x-axis so that f'(c)=0 but the sign of f' does not change.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.fail.c1: a and b must be integers.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.ok.c2: f'(x)=3x²+2ax+b is tangent to the x-axis. There is a c with f'(c)=0, but the sign of f' does not change.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.fail.c2: The discriminant 4a²−12b of f'(x)=3x²+2ax+b is not 0. If it is greater than 0, the sign of f' changes and an extremum appears, and if it is less than 0, there is no c with f'(c)=0.
x-m-h2-09.s.s1.explain: If f'(x)=3x²+2ax+b is tangent to the x-axis (discriminant 4a²−12b=0, that is, a²=3b), then f'(x)=3(x+a/3)²≥0, so even though there is a point where f'=0, f keeps increasing. For example, if a=0, b=0, then f(x)=x³ and f'(0)=0 but there is no extremum.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.prompt: In the functions you made above, f'(c)=0 but there was no extremum. What is the most suitable condition for having an extremum?
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.hint.0: Look at the sign of f'(x) for the function you made in the previous step, to the left and right of c.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the meaning of an extremum (changes from increasing to decreasing, etc.) with each choice.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.o.a: f'(c)=0 and the sign of f' changes on both sides of c
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.r.a: You pointed out that in addition to f'(c)=0, a condition that the increasing and decreasing switch is needed.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.o.b: As long as f'(c)=0, it is always an extremum whatever the sign
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.r.b: In the example you made earlier (f(x)=x³ etc.), f'(0)=0 but there was no extremum.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.o.c: f'(c)=0 and the function value f(c) must also be 0
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.r.c: The value of f(c) has nothing to do with whether there is an extremum. For f(x)=x³+1, f'(0)=0 and f(0)=1, but there is no extremum.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.r.d: If f'(c)>0, the slope of the tangent line at that point is positive, so the function is increasing. It is not a candidate for an extremum.
x-m-h2-09.s.s2.explain: For c to be an extremum, f'(c)=0 and the sign of f' must change on both sides of c (increasing↔decreasing). f'(c)=0 is only a necessary condition for a candidate to be an extremum.

x-m-h2-10.title: Make the probability of a sum on two dice
x-m-h2-10.goal: Count cases to build an event that satisfies a condition yourself, explain why the probabilities are the same, and judge a common misconception.
x-m-h2-10.material: Roll two distinguishable dice (a red one and a blue one) once, and call the sum of the two numbers s. There are 36 cases in all, and each case is equally likely. For example, there is only one case where the sum is 2: (red 1, blue 1).
x-m-h2-10.thinking.0: Build an event that fits the condition
x-m-h2-10.thinking.1: Explain why the probabilities are the same
x-m-h2-10.prereq.0: The meaning of the number of cases
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.prompt: Find two different values of s for which the probability that the sum of the two numbers is s is exactly 1/9 (=4/36). (s is an integer from 2 to 12)
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.hint.0: List one possible (red, blue) each for sums of 4, 5, and 6 and count the number of cases.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.hint.1: Write in a table how the number of cases changes as the sum gets larger.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.ok.c1: s is an integer from 2 to 12.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.fail.c1: s must be an integer from 2 to 12.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.ok.c2: There are 4 cases where the sum is s, so the probability is 4/36=1/9.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.fail.c2: The number of cases where the sum is s is not 4. List and count the ordered pairs that make the sum s.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.explain: The cases where the sum is 5 are (1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1), 4 ways, and the cases where the sum is 9 are (3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3), 4 ways, so both probabilities are 4/36=1/9.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.prompt: What pattern do you see between the two sums, and why are the probabilities the same? Explain.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.hint.0: List all the cases where the sum is 5 as (red, blue) ordered pairs.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.hint.1: If you change each number in the cases you listed to 7 minus that number, what sum does it become? Compare.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.0: Did you actually list the cases where the two sums come up?
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.1: Did you explain ‘why they are the same’ by structure, not by coincidence?
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.selfAssess.2: Did you say how it differs from the sum 7 (6 ways)?
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.model.0: The cases where the sum is 5 are four: (1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1), and the cases where the sum is 9 are four: (3,6),(4,5),(5,4),(6,3). If a number is x, change it to 7−x, and they pair up with each other, so they are symmetric about 7 and the counts are the same.
x-m-h2-10.s.s1.because.model.1: 5 and 9 are each 2 away from 7, so they are symmetric. Each has 4 cases (4/36), so the probabilities are the same.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.prompt: A student said, ‘The probability of a sum of 2 and the probability of a sum of 3 are the same. Both have only one way, like 1+1 and 1+2.’ Which best points out the problem with this reasoning?
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.hint.0: List all the (red, blue) ordered pairs that give sums of 2 and 3.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.hint.1: Among the ordered pairs you listed, compare how many equally likely cases there are for each.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.o.a: The larger the sum, the always larger the probability, so the probabilities of sums 2 and 3 are not the same
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.r.a: The probability does not just keep getting larger as the sum gets larger. Once the sum is past 7, it goes down instead.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.o.b: In 1+2, 2 is greater than 1, so the probability of sum 3 is less than that of sum 2
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.r.b: The probability does not get smaller as the number gets larger.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.o.c: A sum of 3 is two ways, (1,2) and (2,1), and a sum of 2 is only one, (1,1)
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.r.c: The key point is that cases where the numbers on different dice are swapped are counted as different cases.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.o.d: A sum of 2 is even and a sum of 3 is odd, so the two probabilities are different
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.r.d: Odd or even is not the reason the probabilities differ. Sums 3 and 5 are both odd, but their probabilities are different.
x-m-h2-10.s.s2.explain: With distinguishable dice, (1,2) and (2,1) are different cases. A sum of 2 is 1 way (probability 1/36), and a sum of 3 is 2 ways (probability 2/36), so they are not the same. If you count only the ‘number of ways’ by the sum, you miss the cases that are equally likely.
